```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, dpi = 110)
source("../scripts/SNP_analysis.R")
data_file <- "../data/SNPdata.txt"
indCTRL <- 1201:2000
```

This notebook runs the three functions of `scripts/SNP_analysis.R` on the course dataset and looks at what happens at each step: how many SNPs the filters remove, what the HWE and association p-values look like, and why multiple-testing correction matters here. The functions print to the console; that output is hidden below.

## Data

```{r data}
SNPdata <- read.table(data_file, header = TRUE, sep = "\t", row.names = 1)
dim(SNPdata)
table(group = ifelse(seq_len(ncol(SNPdata)) %in% indCTRL, "control", "case"))
table(genotype = unlist(SNPdata), useNA = "ifany")
```

`r nrow(SNPdata)` SNPs, `r length(indCTRL)` controls and `r ncol(SNPdata) - length(indCTRL)` cases, with genotypes coded 0/1/2 and no missing values.

## Quality filters

```{r filters}
invisible(capture.output({
  MAF <- compute_MAF(SNPdata)
  HWE_p <- HWE_test(SNPdata[, indCTRL], tempfile(fileext = ".pdf"))
}))
fail_MAF <- MAF < 0.01
fail_HWE <- HWE_p < 0.01

c(SNPs = nrow(SNPdata),
  fail_MAF = sum(fail_MAF),
  fail_HWE = sum(fail_HWE),
  fail_both = sum(fail_MAF & fail_HWE),
  tested = sum(!fail_MAF & !fail_HWE))
```

- The two filters remove `r sum(fail_MAF | fail_HWE)` SNPs, and they barely overlap (only `r sum(fail_MAF & fail_HWE)` SNP fails both).
- The MAF is computed as the frequency of allele `a` for every SNP, as the instructions require. For `r sum(MAF > 0.5)` SNP this frequency is above 0.5, so `a` is in fact the more common allele there; this does not affect the filter at 0.01.
- `r sum(rowSums(SNPdata[, indCTRL] == 2) == 0)` SNPs have no `aa` genotype among controls. This is the situation the instructions warn about: expected counts stay positive as long as the allele is observed at all, so the HWE test is still defined, and only a monomorphic SNP would give a 0/0 term.

```{r hwe-hist}
hist(HWE_p, breaks = 50, col = "grey80", border = "white",
     main = "HWE test p-values (controls)", xlab = "p-value")
abline(v = 0.01, col = "red", lty = 2)
```

Under Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium the p-values would be roughly uniform. The distribution is indeed broadly flat, and the `r sum(fail_HWE)` SNPs below 0.01 are only slightly more than the ~`r round(0.01 * nrow(SNPdata))` expected by chance: at this threshold the filter mostly removes SNPs that happen to fall in the tail, plus a few genuine departures from equilibrium (possible genotyping errors).

## Association test

```{r association}
# SNP_association_test() writes test_boxplot.pdf to the working directory:
# run it from a temporary folder to keep the notebook folder clean
data_path <- normalizePath(data_file)
old_wd <- setwd(tempdir())
invisible(capture.output(
  res <- SNP_association_test(data_path, indCTRL = indCTRL, MAFth = 0.01, HWEalpha = 0.01)
))
setwd(old_wd)
G <- nrow(res)
c(tested = G,
  `p < 0.05` = sum(res[, "pval"] < 0.05),
  `expected by chance` = round(0.05 * G),
  `q < 0.05` = sum(res[, "qval"] < 0.05))
```

```{r pvals, fig.height = 3.5}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(res[, "pval"], breaks = 50, col = "grey80", border = "white",
     main = "Association p-values", xlab = "p-value")
expected <- -log10(ppoints(G))
observed <- -log10(sort(res[, "pval"]))
plot(expected, observed, pch = 20, cex = 0.6,
     main = "QQ plot", xlab = "expected -log10(p)", ylab = "observed -log10(p)")
abline(0, 1, col = "red")
```

- At p < 0.05, `r sum(res[, "pval"] < 0.05)` SNPs are selected, but about `r round(0.05 * G)` would be selected even if no SNP were associated. Most of the "hits" at this threshold are expected false positives.
- The histogram is flat with a spike near 0, and the QQ plot follows the diagonal before departing sharply in the tail: most SNPs are null, and a minority carry a strong signal.
- Benjamini–Hochberg keeps `r sum(res[, "qval"] < 0.05)` SNPs at q < 0.05, and the count barely changes at q < 0.1 (`r sum(res[, "qval"] < 0.1)`), so the signal is well separated from the background.

The strongest associations, with genotype frequencies per group:

```{r top}
top <- res[order(res[, "pval"])[1:5], ]
freq <- cbind(top[, 1:3] / rowSums(top[, 1:3]), top[, 4:6] / rowSums(top[, 4:6]))
knitr::kable(data.frame(round(freq, 2),
                        pval = format(top[, "pval"], digits = 2),
                        qval = format(top[, "qval"], digits = 2)))
```

The top hits are extreme (p around 1e-54 to 1e-67) and have a large effect: in four of them the `a` allele is rare in controls and far more common in cases (risk allele), while in `chrX_41029224` the pattern is reversed and `aa` is enriched in controls (protective allele).

## Cross-checks

The instructions forbid `chisq.test()` and `p.adjust()` inside the functions, but they are useful to validate the manual implementation.

```{r checks}
chisq_p <- apply(res[, 1:6], 1, function(x) {
  tab <- matrix(x, nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
  tab <- tab[, colSums(tab) > 0, drop = FALSE]   # chisq.test cannot handle empty columns
  suppressWarnings(chisq.test(tab, correct = FALSE)$p.value)
})
empty_class <- (res[, "AA_ctrl"] + res[, "AA_case"] == 0) |
               (res[, "Aa_ctrl"] + res[, "Aa_case"] == 0) |
               (res[, "aa_ctrl"] + res[, "aa_case"] == 0)

c(BH_q_equal = isTRUE(all.equal(unname(res[, "qval"]), unname(p.adjust(res[, "pval"], "BH")))),
  MAF_equal = isTRUE(all.equal(MAF, rowSums(SNPdata) / (2 * ncol(SNPdata)))),
  association_p_equal_all = isTRUE(all.equal(unname(res[, "pval"]), unname(chisq_p))),
  association_p_equal_without_empty_genotype =
    isTRUE(all.equal(unname(res[!empty_class, "pval"]), unname(chisq_p[!empty_class]))))
sum(empty_class)
```

- The Benjamini–Hochberg q-values match `p.adjust()`, and the loop-based MAF matches the one-line vectorised version `rowSums(SNPdata) / (2 * ncol(SNPdata))`.
- The association p-values match `chisq.test()` for all SNPs except the `r sum(empty_class)` where one genotype (always `aa`) is absent in both groups. There the table is effectively 2 × 2 and has 1 degree of freedom, while the function always uses 2, so its p-values for these SNPs are conservative. In this dataset the effect is negligible: with the correct degrees of freedom the number of SNPs at q < 0.05 stays the same.
